concept.name: Agency broker
concept.definition: An agency broker is a broker that executes customer orders strictly as agent — arranging trades with third parties for a disclosed commission — and never takes the other side of the customer's trade as principal. The agency/principal capacity must be disclosed on customer confirmations under Exchange Act Rule 10b-10.
concept.intuition: An agency broker is a pure matchmaker: it finds a counterparty for your trade in the market and charges a commission, without ever selling you anything out of its own pocket.
concept.mechanics: The broker routes the customer's order to an exchange, market maker, or other venue for execution against third-party interest, charging an explicit commission. Because the broker has no inventory position in the trade, it avoids the principal-trade conflicts of markups and trading against the customer, though routing conflicts (payment for order flow) can remain.
concept.failure_modes: Agency status removes principal conflicts but not routing conflicts: order-routing payments and affiliated-venue routing can still compromise execution quality. Agency-only models are also capacity-constrained in illiquid markets where principal risk-taking is what actually finds liquidity.
concept.misconceptions: 'Agency' does not guarantee best execution or the absence of all conflicts — it only means no principal capacity in the trade. Customers also often cannot tell from the fill alone whether the firm acted as agent or principal; the confirmation discloses capacity.
concept.example: An adviser instructs its agency broker to buy 50,000 shares; the broker works the order on exchanges and dark pools against other investors, charges $0.01 per share commission, and buys nothing for its own account.

citations.source: SEC, Division of Trading and Markets, Guide to Broker-Dealer Registration
citations.section: Part II.A-B (broker as agent vs. dealer as principal); Part V.A.4 (capacity disclosure on confirmations)
